articles.title: Per-subscriber vs per-send email pricing, worked out
articles.excerpt: Almost every email tool meters one of two things: how many people are on your list, or how many emails you send them. Which is cheaper is not a matter of opinion. You can work it out with one division…
articles.body: Almost every email tool meters one of two things: how many people are on your list, or how many emails you send them. Which is cheaper is not a matter of opinion. You can work it out with one division. I build an email tool that bills by sends, so I am not neutral here. That is exactly why the arithmetic below is worth doing on your own numbers instead of taking anyone's word for it, mine included. The one number that decides it Take the number of emails you send in a typical month and divide it by the number of people on your list. Call it send intensity. 20,000 subscribers, two campaigns a month to all of them: 40,000 sends over 20,000 subscribers, an intensity of 2. The same list with one campaign every other month: 10,000 over 20,000, an intensity of 0.5.
articles.author: Morten Pradsgaard

articles.title: Same Brakes, Twice the Speed
articles.excerpt: Science, Worked Out — from Arxo. Episode 01. A 1,500 kg car brakes hard from 14 m/s, about 50 km/h, and stops in 14 metres. Same car, same brakes, twice the speed: 28 m/s, about 100 km/h. How far does…
articles.body: Science, Worked Out — from Arxo. Episode 01. A 1,500 kg car brakes hard from 14 m/s, about 50 km/h, and stops in 14 metres. Same car, same brakes, twice the speed: 28 m/s, about 100 km/h. How far does it travel before it stops? Make a guess before you read on. If you said 28 metres, you doubled the distance along with the speed. The worked answer is 56 metres. Twice the speed takes twice the time to stop and four times the distance. Two quantities, two answers The same motion has both a momentum and a kinetic energy. Momentum is mass times velocity: p = mv. Kinetic energy is half the mass times the speed squared: K = ½mv². Double the speed, and they part ways.

articles.title: Learning Dad's Garden: From 4 Minutes of Phone Video to a Printed Watering Sheet, Offline
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass My dad has looked after our pot plants for years. On Sunday morning he filmed them on his phone and explained ea…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass My dad has looked after our pot plants for years. On Sunday morning he filmed them on his phone and explained each pot as he went. At the bush with tag 12, he said: "Give regular amount of water, the usual amount." He knows exactly how much that is. I didn't. So I built a tool that finds every line like that and asks him. It's called Learning Dad's Garden. It turns his walk-through into a printed checklist I can take outside. Each pot gets a row, with a tick box for each day it needs something. Gemma 4 does the reading, on my laptop. Before anything prints, Dad answers the questions a beginner would ask. What I Built I'm taking up Dad's hobby, and he knows what every pot needs.

articles.title: EvidenceFlip: Do Frontier LLMs Know When Not to Answer?
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge EvidenceFlip is a deterministic benchmark of evidence-grounded decision-making. Each case su…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge EvidenceFlip: Measuring Epistemic Calibration in Language Models Under Source Conflict and Pressure Submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Abstract EvidenceFlip is a deterministic benchmark of evidence-grounded decision-making. Each case supplies a question and labeled evidence snippets. The model returns one JSON object with an action: answer when the evidence supports a single answer, abstain when the requested fact is unsupported, or flag_conflict when credible sources are incompatible. Cases are grouped by category, including conflict and pressure, where the prompt pushes the model to answer despite missing support. Scoring uses no LLM judge. abstain and flag_conflict cases score 1 for the correct action.

articles.title: Trailside: An Offline Field Guide Powered by Gemma 4, Ollama and Open Weights
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Trailside is a field guide that lives on your own laptop. You point your phone at a leaf, a mushroom, a bird or…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Trailside is a field guide that lives on your own laptop. You point your phone at a leaf, a mushroom, a bird or a beetle, snap a photo, and an open-weight model tells you what it probably is, how sure it is, what it could be confused with, and whether you should keep your hands off it. Every sighting goes into a field journal you can export as markdown. The part I care about most is the last line of every answer: a look-up challenge . Instead of ending with "here's more to read", Trailside ends with one thing to go and check in person, like "count the lobes on the next leaf of this tree" or "stand still for a minute and see if you can hear it again".

articles.title: I built a 3D playground to see how AI understands words - WordCanvas3D
articles.excerpt: To a language model, the word "cat" is just a long list of numbers. So is "dog". So is "democracy". What surprised me is that those numbers aren't random. Words with similar meanings end up close to e…
articles.body: To a language model, the word "cat" is just a long list of numbers. So is "dog". So is "democracy". What surprised me is that those numbers aren't random. Words with similar meanings end up close to each other, and some relationships even turn into directions you can do math with. I wanted to actually see that, not just read about it. So I built WordCanvas3D . 🔗 Try it: https://wordcanvas3d.vercel.app/ 💻 Code: https://github.com/Akage1234/WordCanvas3D It's free, open source, and runs in your browser. No signup. Here's what you can explore. Fly through a map of meaning Every point is a word. Grab the scene, spin it around, zoom in, and you start noticing neighborhoods: animals near animals, countries near countries, emotions near emotions.

articles.excerpt: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission,…
articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission. One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes.
